I.	It was a wonderful night, such a night as is only possible when we are young, dear reader. The sky
was so starry, so bright that, looking at it, one could not help asking oneself whether ill-humoured
and capricious people could live under such a sky. That is a youthful question too, dear reader,
very youthful, but may the Lord put it more frequently into your heart.
From early morning I had been oppressed by a strange despondency. It suddenly seemed to me
that I was lonely, that everyone was forsaking me and going away from me. For though I had been
living almost eight years in Petersburg I had hardly an acquaintance. But what did I want with
acquaintances? I was acquainted with all Petersburg as it was; that was why I felt as though they
were all deserting me when all Petersburg packed up and went to its summer villa.
I know the houses too. As I walk along they seem to run forward in the streets to look out at me
from every window, and almost to say: “Good-morning! How do you do? I am quite well, thank
God, and I am to have a new storey in May,” or, “How are you? I am being redecorated to-morrow;”
or, “I was almost burnt down and had such a fright,” and so on. I have my favourites among them,
some are dear friends. One of them intends to be treated by the architect this summer. I shall go
every day on purpose to see that the operation is not a failure.

Il.	The house had grown old in its silence, like a woman aging without the grace of youth. Eleanor
pushed open the creaking door, her lantern casting trembling shadows against the walls. The air
tasted of dust and forgotten time. She had come searching for her sister, who had vanished three
weeks prior under circumstances that the town preferred not to discuss. The locals called the
mansion "cursed," but Eleanor knew better—curses were merely explanations for things people
could not understand. The servants had long abandoned their posts; the kitchen held no warmth.
In the parlor, she found a leather journal, its pages yellowed and brittle. The handwriting within
was frantic, documenting observations of something that moved through the halls after dark,
something that whispered her sister's name. The entries grew increasingly incoherent, the
author's fear palpable in every crossed-out word. Eleanor's hands trembled as she read by
candlelight. The final entry was dated the night her sister disappeared: "It knows me now. It calls,
and I must answer." What Eleanor discovered next would haunt her forever—a door beneath the
stairs, previously invisible, now standing ajar. Behind it lay nothing but an impenetrable darkness
and the faint echo of a familiar voice calling her name.
Source: A Whisper at Midnight; Book by Darcy Burke

IV.	The garden had belonged to the Chowdhury family for seven generations, a small plot of earth in
Mumbai where jasmine vines climbed white walls and crows nested in the old neem tree. Maya
returned to it after fifteen years of living abroad, expecting nostalgia. Instead, she found
bewilderment. Everything was smaller than she remembered—the garden she had imagined as
vast now seemed confined, almost suffocating in its smallness. Her grandfather sat in the
courtyard as he always had, though age had rendered him nearly unrecognizable. His hands, once
strong enough to coax blooms from stubborn soil, trembled as he tended the plants. He did not
acknowledge her arrival; perhaps he did not recognize her. Maya wandered through the garden,
touching the familiar plants, and noticed something strange: the flowers were blooming in the
wrong season, their colors muted and peculiar. The gardener, old Ranjit, spoke to her in hushed
tones that evening. He told her that her grandfather had not spoken a word in three years, that he
spent every night under the neem tree, whispering to the darkness. Ranjit believed the garden
was dying, that something fundamental had shifted in the earth itself. When Maya finally
approached her grandfather to embrace him, he recoiled. As she stood there, rejected and
bewildered, she understood that she had lost not just the garden of her childhood but the
grandfather she thought she knew.
Source: The Secret Garden; Novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett

Mumbai where jasmine vines climbed white walls and crows nested in the old neem tree. Maya
returned to it after fifteen years of living abroad, expecting nostalgia. Instead, she found
bewilderment. Everything was smaller than she remembered—the garden she had imagined as
vast now seemed confined, almost suffocating in its smallness. Her grandfather sat in the
courtyard as he always had, though age had rendered him nearly unrecognizable. His hands, once
strong enough to coax blooms from stubborn soil, trembled as he tended the plants. He did not
acknowledge her arrival; perhaps he did not recognize her. Maya wandered through the garden,
touching the familiar plants, and noticed something strange: the flowers were blooming in the
wrong season, their colors muted and peculiar. The gardener, old Ranjit, spoke to her in hushed
tones that evening. He told her that her grandfather had not spoken a word in three years, that he
spent every night under the neem tree, whispering to the darkness. Ranjit believed the garden
was dying, that something fundamental had shifted in the earth itself. When Maya finally
approached her grandfather to embrace him, he recoiled. As she stood there, rejected and
bewildered, she understood that she had lost not just the garden of her childhood but the
grandfather she thought she knew.
Source: The Secret Garden; Novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett

tiger, lion and leopard — within its forests, a rare ecological occurrence. www.lawpreptutorial.com

VIII. The Nazi regime made systematic and strategic use of language and media to advance its ideology
and consolidate public support. Official communications deliberately avoided direct words such as
“kill” or “murder,” replacing them with misleading and euphemistic terms that concealed the
reality of mass violence. Expressions like “special treatment,” “final solution” for Jews,
“euthanasia” for the disabled, and “selection” or “disinfection” were employed to normalise and
obscure acts of killing. Deportations to gas chambers were referred to as “evacuations,” while the
gas chambers themselves were labelled “disinfection areas” and designed to resemble bathrooms
with fake showerheads, further masking their true purpose.
Alongside this manipulation of language, the regime used media extensively to popularise its
worldview. Visual imagery, films, radio broadcasts, posters, slogans, and leaflets were used to
spread Nazi ideas and shape public opinion. Groups identified as enemies of the state were
stereotyped, mocked, and portrayed as dangerous or evil. Socialists and liberals were depicted as
weak and corrupt, while Jews were systematically dehumanised through propaganda, most
notably in films such as *The Eternal Jew*. These portrayals aimed to inflame emotions, redirect
public anger, and legitimise persecution of those labelled as “undesirable.”
Source: Excerpts from NCERT History Textbook, Class IX, India and the Contemporary World — I,
Chapter: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler, National Council of Educational Research and Training,

questions.stimulus:
XI.	In the landmark judgment of State of UP v. Ajmal Beg, the Supreme Court of India expressed
grave concern over the "institutionalized evil" of dowry, which persists despite legal prohibitions.
The Bench observed that dowry has morphed from a voluntary practice intended for a woman's
financial independence into a mechanism for material extraction. The Court emphasized that this
practice is fundamentally at odds with the constitutional values of justice, liberty, and fraternity,
directly violating Article 14’s guarantee of equality by treating women as sources of financial gain.
The case involved the dowry death of a 20-year-old woman, married for just over a year, who was
subjected to persistent demands for a motorcycle, electronics, and cash. While the Allahabad High
Court had previously acquitted the accused—reasoning that their poverty made such demands
improbable—the Supreme Court set aside this acquittal. The Bench clarified that the Dowry
Prohibition Act makes no distinction between demands made before or after marriage and
asserted that financial status does not negate the probability of dowry harassment. Consequently,
the conviction of the husband and his mother was restored, though the Court refrained from
incarcerating the 94-year-old mother-in-law due to her age.
Significantly, the Court noted that dowry is a systemic issue prevalent across all religions in the
subcontinent. It observed that in some communities, dowry has been adopted alongside nominal
religious gifts like mehr, hollowing out the original protective purpose of such customs. To address
this social conditioning, the Court issued a series of directives, including:
Incorporating constitutional values of equality into educational curricula.
Ensuring the effective appointment and visibility of Dowry Prohibition Officers.
Sensitizing police and judicial officers to the psychological dimensions of dowry cases.
Expediting long-pending trials under Sections 304B (dowry death) and 498A (cruelty) of the IPC.
Ultimately, the Court underscored that true independence necessitates social transformation,
urging authorities to eradicate entrenched customs that undermine the dignity and financial
security of women.

gifts: Supreme Court issues slew of directions to tighten law enforcement

XII. In the law of torts, liability is typically categorized as either fault-based or no-fault. Under no-fault
liability, a defendant is held accountable for damages even in the absence of negligence or intent.
This concept is divided into two primary doctrines: Strict Liability and Absolute Liability.

dictates that if a person brings onto their land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, they

taken. For this rule to apply, three essentials must be met: the defendant must bring a hazardous
substance onto their property, there must be a "non-natural" use of the land, and the substance
must actually escape the premises and cause harm.
However, Strict Liability is not an exhaustive rule and provides some specific defenses:
1. Plaintiffs Own Fault: If the damage resulted from the plaintiff's own trespassing or
negligence.

2. Act of God: Unforeseeable and uncontrollable natural disasters.
8. Volenti Non-Fit Injuria: If the dangerous substance was maintained for the mutual benefit of
both parties.
4. Act of a Stranger: If a third party over whom the defendant had no control caused the escape.

questions.stimulus:
XIII. The Indian Constitution is anchored by a triad of fundamental provisions collectively known as
the "Golden Triangle": Articles 14, 19, and 21. Rather than existing as isolated legal mandates,
these articles form an interconnected web that serves as the ultimate bulwark against arbitrary
state action and the primary protector of individual dignity. The concept of the Golden Triangle
emphasizes that these rights are mutually reinforcing; the deprivation of one often leads to the
erosion of the others.
Article 14 establishes the foundational principle of equality, guaranteeing "equality before the
law" and "equal protection of the laws." It prohibits the State from discriminating on grounds such
as religion, race, caste, or sex. Landmark rulings, such as Keshavananda Bharati (1973), have
recognized this right to equality as part of the Constitution's "basic structure," meaning it cannot
be abrogated even by constitutional amendments.
Article 19 delineates the essential freedoms of a citizen, including speech, assembly, movement,
and profession. While these freedoms are vital for a functional democracy, they are not absolute.
The State may impose "reasonable restrictions" on grounds like national security or public order.
However, as established in Romesh Thappar (1950), the threshold for these restrictions is high,
ensuring that even unpopular critiques of the government remain protected.
Article 21is the most evolved provision, safeguarding the right to life and personal liberty.
Initially interpreted narrowly, the landmark Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) case

fundamentally transformed its scope. The Court ruled that any "procedure established by law"
used to deprive a person of liberty must not be arbitrary, but must be "just, fair, and
reasonable." This decision effectively synthesized the three articles, holding that a law under
Article 21 must also pass the tests of Article 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Article 19
(reasonableness).
The interdependence of the Triangle is best seen in modern judicial expansions, where the "right
to life" now encompasses the right to privacy (Puttaswamy), a clean environment, and even
emergency medical care. A notable application is the "Golden Hour" principle, where the judiciary
linked Article 21 to the mandatory duty of healthcare providers to treat accident victims, ensuring
that dignity and life are prioritized over procedural formalities.
Ultimately, the Golden Triangle represents the democratic essence of India. It ensures that the
administration of justice is not merely a matter of following rules, but a commitment to upholding
a triad of values—equality, freedom, and dignity—that are indispensable to the human
experience.

questions.stimulus:
XIV. On July 1, 2024, India transitioned from its colonial-era criminal justice framework to a modern,
indigenous system with the enforcement of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). These laws
replaced the Indian Penal Code (1860), the Code of Criminal Procedure (1973), and the Indian
Evidence Act (1872), respectively. A central theme of this overhaul is the "decolonization" of law
and the integration of technology into the judicial process.
Under the BNSS, procedural efficiency has been prioritized through mandated timelines. For
instance, Section 173 of the BNSS mandates that a preliminary inquiry must be conducted within
14 days in cases punishable with 3 to 7 years of imprisonment. Furthermore, the law now allows
for the registration of a "Zero FIR" at any police station, regardless of the area of jurisdiction,
ensuring that victims are not turned away due to territorial technicalities. The BNS has also
redefined several offenses. Notably, "Sedition" (formerly Section 124A of the IPC) has been
replaced by Section 152, which penalizes "acts endangering sovereignty, unity, and integrity of
India." Unlike the old law, Section 152 explicitly excludes "comments made in good faith or in a

reasonable manner" regarding government action, focusing instead on secessionist activities or
armed rebellion.
Crucially, the BSA has expanded the definition of evidence. Under Section 61 of the BSA,
electronic or digital records are now categorized as "primary evidence," whereas they were
previously often treated as secondary evidence requiring stringent certification. In a 2025 ruling,
the Supreme Court clarified that while electronic evidence is primary, the procedural safeguards
under the BSA—such as ensuring the integrity of the storage device—must be strictly followed to
prevent tampering. The Court noted that the transition to the new laws is "prospective," meaning
crimes committed before July 1, 2024, will continue to be tried under the old IPC/CrPC, while new
offenses fall under the BNS/BNSS.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from The Criminal Law Reform Analysis, November
2025

questions.stimulus:
XVI. India's Urban Mobility Crisis: India stands at a critical crossroads. Its urban centers are
growing rapidly with more people buying private vehicles, creating severe traffic congestion, air
pollution, and a declining quality of life. This crisis did not happen by accident—it is the direct
result of decades of planning that prioritized cars over public transportation. Most Indian cities
have focused heavily on building metro rail systems while neglecting buses and other transport
modes. This "one size fits all" approach has created serious problems: areas without metro
coverage have almost no transit options, forcing people to buy cars and motorcycles.
The real issue is that governments have been moving cars, not people. A city like Bengaluru has
more buses per mile than most cities, yet it performs poorly compared to international standards
because it lacks good last-mile connectivity and pedestrian-friendly streets. Projects like tunnel
roads and coastal highways seem smart temporarily because they reduce traffic, but they
ultimately invite more vehicles onto the roads—a phenomenon called "induced demand."
Meanwhile, cities are destroying valuable public spaces for these projects without solving the
actual problem. www.lawpreptutorial.com
However, there are positive signs. Survey data shows that most people are willing to use quality
public transportation if available. Metro systems are expanding rapidly, and some cities are
redesigning streets with wide pedestrian paths. Bengaluru plans to deploy 10,000 buses in coming
years. For real progress, citizens must demand better urban planning from their governments and
choose public transit over personal vehicles. Only a fundamental mindset shift from "moving cars"
to "moving people" can create the liveable cities India needs.
Source: The Journal Club (Bit News), September 2025; India's Urban Mobility Crisis

questions.stimulus:
XVIII. Facial Recognition and Digital Privacy Concerns: As artificial intelligence advances, facial
recognition technology has become increasingly powerful and accessible. Governments and private
companies can now identify individuals in crowds, track movement patterns, and monitor
behaviour with minimal human oversight. This creates unprecedented privacy risks. Consider
what happens when facial recognition is used without consent at airports, shopping malls, or
public protests: individuals lose the ability to move through public spaces anonymously. In
authoritarian regimes, this technology enables mass surveillance systems that suppress dissent
and control populations. Even in democracies, the absence of clear consent mechanisms means
people cannot opt out of being scanned and tracked.
The core problem is that current regulations lag far behind the technology's capabilities. Data
protection laws often require consent before collecting personal information, but facial recognition
systems operate silently and invisibly. A person walking down the street has no way to know if
their face has been captured, analyzed, and stored in a database. This asymmetry of power—
where authorities can watch citizens but citizens cannot know they are being watched—
undermines the basic principles of democratic society. Facial recognition technology also amplifies
bias: studies show that these systems are significantly less accurate for people with darker skin
tones, creating disparities in both surveillance and error rates.
Addressing this crisis requires explicit legal protections: banning facial recognition in sensitive
contexts like protests and public spaces, requiring transparent reporting of surveillance activities,
and building independent oversight mechanisms to review government access to biometric data.
Without strong regulatory action, facial recognition will become a tool for unchecked state and
corporate power, fundamentally changing the relationship between individuals and institutions.
Source: Online, December 2025 & OHCHR Joint Declaration on AI
